blocks.h2: Spend the budget where the miles are
blocks.html:
If the budget only stretches to one good item, make it the S1P safety trainer — certified toe cap and midsole in a package light enough to walk all shift (what the codes mean). Add cushioned wicking socks and replace insoles when they flatten; a £10 insole outperforms a £70 trainer with a dead one.

Posted to chill or freezer aisles? That's a different kit problem — lined trousers, thermal base layer, insulated gloves, and for freezer work a rated coldstore suit. The warehouse sector guide maps kit to every zone.

faq.q: What footwear is best for warehouse picking?
faq.a: An S1P safety trainer — the same certified toe cap and midsole as a boot at a fraction of the weight, which matters when a picking shift covers 15 km on concrete. Add cushioned wicking socks and refresh the insoles regularly.

faq.q: Do warehouse operatives need hi-vis?
faq.a: Almost always — most operations mandate at least a Class 1 or 2 vest anywhere mechanical handling equipment runs, which in practice means everywhere past the entrance. The site induction sets the exact class; the vest-on-at-the-door rule is standard.

faq.q: What should I wear for a cold store shift?
faq.a: Chill aisles: thermal base layer, lined trousers and insulated gloves over the standard kit. Freezer chambers (−18 °C and below) need a rated EN 342 coldstore suit, insulated CI-rated footwear and covered ears — that kit is normally employer-issued.

pages.cardBlurb: Where arc-flash clothing actually applies, what the IEC 61482 label tells you, and the melt-layer rule that voids it all.
pages.h1: PPE for electricians: the arc-flash line.
pages.metaTitle: PPE for Electricians: Arc Flash Clothing Explained | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: When electricians need arc-rated clothing, what IEC 61482 classes and ATPV values mean on a label, the no-synthetics layering rule, and the kit list either side of the line.
pages.lede: Most domestic and commercial electrical work never meets an arc-flash risk assessment — and some industrial work meets it every day. Electricians' kit splits cleanly along that line, so this guide covers both sides of it and the label that marks the boundary.

blocks.h2: Which side of it are you on?
blocks.html:
Below the line — installation, second fix, domestic and most commercial work on dead, isolated circuits: the kit is ordinary quality trade wear. Stretch work trousers, polos, S1P or S3 footwear, and dexterity-first gloves. Safe isolation is the protection; the clothing just has to work.

Above the line — live testing and fault-finding on industrial systems, switchgear operation, work near energised LV/HV equipment where the employer's risk assessment identifies arc-flash potential: clothing becomes PPE in the legal sense. That means arc-rated garments to IEC 61482, worn as a complete system.

Who decides? The risk assessment, not the wearer. If your work order involves energised switchgear, the arc assessment (and the PPE it specifies) should arrive with it.

blocks.lead: Two test routes appear on labels — a garment may carry either or both.
head: Marking
Test behind it
What it tells you
rows: The common spec for utility and industrial switching
Rated thermal performance — matched to the calculated incident energy of your task
Usually certified alongside arc on multi-norm garments

blocks.html: The layer under the arc kit can undo the arc kit. Synthetic base layers melt at arc temperatures — inside the garment that just protected you. Under arc-rated clothing wear arc-rated or natural-fibre layers only, and that includes the T-shirt. The same rule runs through all FR work — the energy sector guide covers the system.

Arc-rated clothing protects the body; the task-specific items are their own standards: insulating gloves for live work certify separately (with leather over-protectors and periodic retest), face shields and balaclavas carry their own arc ratings, and footwear for electrical environments avoids exposed metal — many electricians run composite-cap, metal-free boots as standard anyway (the cap comparison).

For the everyday tools-and-testing kit below the line: hard-wearing trousers with holster pockets, embroidered polos for the customer-facing side, and gloves you'll actually keep on — the EN 388 decoder sorts those.

faq.q: Do all electricians need arc flash clothing?
faq.a: No — the requirement follows the risk assessment, not the trade. Work on dead, isolated circuits doesn't create arc PPE requirements; live testing, fault-finding and switchgear operation on industrial systems commonly do. If the assessment identifies arc risk, it must also specify the rated clothing.

faq.q: What does ATPV mean on arc flash clothing?
faq.a: Arc Thermal Performance Value, in calories per square centimetre — the incident energy at which the garment gives a 50% probability of preventing a second-degree burn. The employer's arc calculation for the task sets the cal/cm² the clothing must meet or exceed.

faq.q: What is the difference between APC Class 1 and Class 2?
faq.a: Both come from the IEC 61482 box test: Class 1 tests against a 4 kA arc, Class 2 against 7 kA. Class 2 is the common specification for utility switching and industrial LV work — but the right class comes from the risk assessment.

faq.q: Can I wear a normal T-shirt under arc-rated overalls?
faq.a: Only if it's natural fibre — cotton at minimum, arc-rated ideally. Polyester and blends melt at arc temperatures and cause severe injury inside otherwise-intact protective clothing. The no-synthetics rule applies to every layer, base included.

heroImage.alt: Electrician in gloves and safety glasses working in a control panel

blocks.html:
Starting out and buying your own? The order that pays: shoes first — a slip on a wet tile ends more kitchen careers than any burn, and a proper SR-soled kitchen shoe is the one item with no cheap substitute. Jackets second, three of them, because a chef in a stained jacket gets judged before the food does. Trousers third — two pairs get you through while you learn what cut suits the heat of your section. Everything else can be house-issued or accumulated.

On the laundering that keeps whites white and logos intact through the boil washes: the branded-kit wash guide covers it.

items.l: Lightweight jackets with vented backs exist — grill sections still want the heavier shield
Synthetics conduct heat and melt; cotton insulates and survives the wash — same reason as industry FR
A dry jacket after the lunch rush beats any technical fabric claim

faq.q: How many chef jackets do you need?
faq.a: Three is the working minimum for a five-shift week with home laundering — one on, one in the wash, one dry. Busy kitchens and doubles push it to four or five. Trousers follow at two to three pairs.

faq.q: What shoes do chefs wear?
faq.a: Closed shoes with liquid-shedding uppers and a slip-rated (SR) sole — wet, greasy floors are the kitchen's biggest injury source. Clog and trainer styles both work; the sole rating and the closed top are the non-negotiables.

faq.q: Why do chefs wear loose trousers?
faq.a: Scald protection: loose fabric pulls away from the leg when hot liquid hits, while tight fabric presses it against skin. Add the airflow benefit at a 40 °C pass and the traditional baggy cut earns its look.

faq.q: What should a commis chef buy first?
faq.a: Slip-rated kitchen shoes, then three jackets, then trousers. Shoes prevent the injury that ends shifts; jackets carry your presentability; everything else can accumulate or be house-issued.

blocks.h2: S3 for the site, S5 for the hole
blocks.html:
No single boot survives groundworks. The S3 leather boot handles the general site day — walking, machine spotting, kerb lines. The moment the work goes into water, wet concrete or serious mud, it's the S5 safety wellington: waterproof by construction, with the same toe cap, midsole and cleated sole (codes explained). Wet concrete specifically is a chemical burn hazard — wellingtons with trousers over the top, not tucked in, is the pour-day setup.

Both pairs die faster in this trade than any other: mud draws the oils out of leather, so the boot-care routine — mud off same day, never radiator-dried — is worth reading twice.

items.l: Waterproofs that wet out usually need treatment, not binning
If the warm layer covers the fluoro, the warm layer must be hi-vis
The cheapest morale insurance in construction

blocks.html: The employer-side view — baselines and trade tables — lives in the construction sector guide; jacket recovery in reproofing waterproofs.

faq.q: What boots do groundworkers need?
faq.a: Two pairs: S3 leather boots for general site work, and S5 safety wellingtons for excavations, mud and concrete pours. Wet concrete is a chemical burn hazard as well as a soaking — wellingtons with waterproof trousers over the top is the pour-day standard.

faq.q: Why do groundworkers wear Class 3 hi-vis?
faq.a: The trade lives around moving plant — excavators slewing, tippers reversing, deliveries arriving — often in poor light and weather. Class 3's larger fluorescent and reflective areas fit that exposure, and many groundworks contractors mandate it with hi-vis trousers.

faq.q: Are knee pads worth it for groundworks?
faq.a: They're the item veterans most wish they'd worn from day one. Kerb laying, ducting and drainage mean hours kneeling on aggregate; trouser-insert pads or strap-ons prevent the cumulative damage that shows up years later.

That's a real specification, and here's the kit that meets it.

blocks.h2: Bare below the elbow, and what it means for kit
blocks.html:
Most care providers run a bare-below-the-elbow policy during personal care: short sleeves, no wristwatch, minimal rings — because forearms and cuffs are what touch people and surfaces, and they're what handwashing has to reach. For the wardrobe, that means short-sleeved tunics as the base garment and warm layers designed to come off easily and go back on between tasks, not knitwear worn through care duties.

The other policy reality is laundering: uniforms need washing at the temperature policy states — commonly 60 °C — which is why care tunics are poly-cotton blends built for it, and why three to five sets isn't generous, it's the minimum that lets a worker change after a soiled shift and still have kit for tomorrow.

blocks.h2: Three details that matter in practice

items.l: Trim and colour coding tell residents and families who's who at a glance
Phones, gloves, pens, keys — tunic pocket layout is a genuine selection criterion
Printed name badges peel in hot washes; stitched names don't

blocks.html: The employer-side view — settings, laundering benchmarks and support-staff kit — is in the healthcare sector guide. For team orders with colour-coding and embroidery, talk to us.

faq.q: How many tunics do care staff need?
faq.a: Three to five, assuming uniforms are washed after each shift as most policies require. Fewer than three means a single soiled shift breaks the rotation. Trousers follow at two to three pairs.

faq.q: What does bare below the elbow mean?
faq.a: During personal care tasks: short sleeves, no wristwatch or bracelets, and minimal rings, so hands and forearms can be washed effectively and cuffs don't transfer between people. Kit-wise it means short-sleeved tunics as standard and warm layers that come off easily between tasks.

faq.q: What shoes are best for care work?
faq.a: Washable uppers, slip-rated soles, closed toes and real cushioning. Care shifts run long on hard floors and involve spills — trainers-style washable shoes purpose-made for healthcare do the job; fabric fashion trainers don't survive the mop-bucket reality.

faq.q: Can care staff wear cardigans or fleeces?
faq.a: Usually yes for corridors, handover and breaks — coded to the uniform — but off during personal care under bare-below-the-elbow policies. Buy layers on that assumption: easy on, easy off, washable with the rest of the kit.

pages.lede: A workshop hands you three hazards on rotation: oil on everything, edges under everything, and assemblies that spin. The kit list answers all three — and the golden rule is that nothing loose goes near the third one.

blocks.h2: Nothing loose near anything that spins
blocks.html:
Serpentine belts, prop shafts, wheel balancers, bench grinders — a workshop is full of assemblies that grab. The rule is absolute: cuffs closed, zips done, no dangling drawstrings, no rings, and gloves off at specific rotating machines where a snagged glove pulls the hand in. It's why proper workshop coveralls have elasticated or stud cuffs and covered zips, and why the baggy-hoodie look has no place under a ramp.

On the oil itself: it's coming for the kit regardless. Two coveralls in rotation, washed hot with a degreaser pre-treat — the oil & grease guide is written for exactly this wardrobe. Kit that stays saturated stops being workwear and starts being a skin-contact problem; engine oils and dermatitis are a known pair, which is also why the gloves matter beyond grip.

items.l: A washed coverall weekly beats one worn to saturation
Mineral oil on skin daily is a dermatitis plan — interrupt it
For fluids work — brake cleaner and used oil aren't handwash

faq.q: Should mechanics wear coveralls or trousers and top?
faq.a: Coveralls win under ramps and inside engine bays — one garment, no waist gap, snug cuffs, industrial-washable. Two-piece suits MOT testing and customer-facing bays. Either way: two sets in rotation, because oil accumulates faster than one wash cycle.

faq.q: What gloves are best for mechanics?
faq.a: Nitrile-coated work gloves for general spannering — nitrile keeps grip through oil where PU and latex fail — plus disposable nitrile for fluids. At specific rotating machinery, gloves come off entirely: a snagged glove pulls the hand in.

faq.q: How do you get oil out of mechanic overalls?
faq.a: Pre-treat with a degreaser (neat washing-up liquid works), wait 20–30 minutes, then wash on the hottest cycle the label allows with heavy-duty detergent. Air-dry and check before tumble-drying — heat sets residual oil. Saturated kit that won't come clean gets retired.

faq.q: Do mechanics need safety boots?
faq.a: Yes — dropped tools, brake discs and trolley jack handles settle the argument. S1P covers workshop floors; step up to S3 if the job includes yards and recovery work in the weather. Metal-free composite caps suit anyone working around live electrics on EVs.

heroImage.alt: Mechanic in blue coveralls and grip gloves working under a car on a lift

blocks.h2: The kit check that happens at the gate
blocks.html:
Trackside access controls actually inspect clothing, and the failures are predictable: faded orange that's drifted toward peach, cracked or peeling tape, and jackets past their wash count. The hi-vis care rules apply with extra teeth here — velcro closed in the wash, no softener, retire on fade — because the garment isn't just PPE, it's your ticket through the gate.

Layering follows the same logic as everywhere else with one rail twist: every visible layer is orange. A yellow vest over an orange jacket, or a black fleece zipped over the lot, both fail. Warm layers go under the certified orange shell.

items.l: Confirm class and trouser requirements with the PC before ordering
Wet possessions and no drying time — rotation is compliance
Logos must stay clear of certified areas on rail garments too

faq.q: What hi-vis do you need for trackside rail work?
faq.a: Orange garments certified to EN ISO 20471 meeting the rail spec (RIS-3279-TOM) — in practice a Class 3 orange jacket, with orange trousers mandated by most principal contractors on possessions. Yellow is non-compliant on or near the line.

faq.q: What boots are best for ballast?
faq.a: S3 boots with genuine ankle support — ballast is the ankle-turning surface, and the S3 midsole handles the through-sole hazards of trackside debris. Waterproof versions (S7 or S3 WR) earn their price on night possessions.

faq.q: Can you wear a fleece over rail hi-vis?
faq.a: Not over it — covering the orange removes the certified visible area, and access controls will pick it up. Warm layers go underneath; if the outer layer is the warm layer, it must itself be certified orange rail-spec.

pages.cardBlurb: EN ISO 11393 protection explained — trouser types and classes, chainsaw boots, and the helmet system that comes as a set.
pages.h1: Chainsaw & forestry kit: protection with a class number.
pages.metaTitle: Chainsaw & Forestry Kit: EN ISO 11393 Explained | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Chainsaw PPE decoded — EN ISO 11393 trouser types A and C, protection classes by chain speed, chainsaw boots, and the helmet-visor-ear-defender system worn as one unit.
pages.lede: Chainsaw clothing is unusual among PPE: it's designed to be destroyed. The layers inside a protective trouser exist to pull out, clog the sprocket and stall the chain in the fraction of a second before it reaches the leg. That design has types and classes — and choosing them wrong defeats the idea.

blocks.html:
Inside chainsaw-protective garments sit layers of long, loose fibres. On contact, the chain rips them out and drags them into the drive sprocket, jamming the saw to a stop — sacrificing the garment to save the limb. Three consequences follow:

  • One contact and the garment is finished. Even a nick that doesn't reach skin has pulled the protective layers; it's replaced, not sewn up.
  • Protection is rated to chain speed — the classes below — because faster chains need more fibre and more stopping.
  • It only works where the layers are. That's the difference between the trouser types: coverage pattern.

blocks.h2: The two decisions on the label
head: Decision
Options
How to choose
rows: Type A — front of legs · Type C — all-round
Type A for ground work with escape routes; Type C for climbing, platform and utility work where the saw can reach the back of the leg
Class 1 (20 m/s) · Class 2 (24 m/s) · Class 3 (28 m/s)
Match to the saw's chain speed — Class 1 covers most ground-based forestry saws; professional users check the saw's plate
Toe cap plus chainsaw-protective layers over the vamp — ordinary S3 boots are not chainsaw boots
The left hand rides nearest the bar on most saws

blocks.h2: The helmet is a system, worn complete
blocks.html:
The forestry helmet set — shell, mesh visor, ear defenders — is designed as one unit and worn as one: chip strike, noise and canopy debris arrive together. Hi-vis shells are the forestry norm so ground crews stay visible among the trees, and helmets carry a service life (check the moulding date) that outdoor UV shortens.

Around the protective kit goes ordinary outdoor workwear logic: wicking base layers, hi-vis where extraction machinery operates, and waterproofs maintained so a wet day doesn't end the layering system. Cut-resistant gloves for the non-saw handling — sharpening, dragging brash — follow the EN 388 ratings.

Training is part of the PPE. Chainsaw clothing assumes competent technique — it's the last line, not the plan. UK chainsaw users need appropriate training and assessment (Lantra/NPTC routes are the recognised ones), and employers must provide both the kit and the competence. A Class 3 trouser on an untrained operator is not a safety system.

faq.q: What is the difference between Type A and Type C chainsaw trousers?
faq.a: Coverage: Type A protects the front of the legs and is the ground-work standard; Type C wraps protection all round the leg for climbing, platform and utility arborists where the saw can reach from any angle. Type C is hotter and heavier — that's the trade.

faq.q: What do chainsaw protection classes mean?
faq.a: They're rated stopping speeds under EN ISO 11393: Class 1 to 20 m/s of chain speed, Class 2 to 24, Class 3 to 28. Match the class to the saw you run — Class 1 covers most ground-based forestry work; check the saw's specification plate.

faq.q: Can you repair chainsaw trousers after a cut?
faq.a: No — any chain contact that pulls the internal fibres has spent the protection, even if the outer looks repairable. The garment is replaced. Sewing up the shell hides the fact that the layers underneath are gone.

faq.q: Do you need special boots for chainsaw work?
faq.a: Yes — chainsaw boots certified to EN ISO 17249, which add chainsaw-protective layers over the vulnerable areas on top of a standard safety-boot toe cap. Ordinary S3 site boots provide no chain protection at all.

heroImage.alt: Chainsaw protection trousers and forestry kit
